mandate: Pilot-approved bracket 4; maximize power, consistency and menace (data/decks/ur-dragon/pilot_feedback.md).
archetype: Five-colour Dragon critical-mass battlecruiser with a certified combo exit: 24 bodies of which 22 are Dragons feeding per-Dragon triggers, on top of three contained two-card infinites that all route through Aggravated Assault. deck-audit runs it on the combo budget (4-8 tutors, 4-6 protection) and the deck sits inside both — but the measured rate of the infinite is 3.6% by turn six, so the median game is won by Dragons and burn, not by the loop.

role_assignment.default_role: Control-leaning engine seat. The deck owns the long game (strategy:whos-the-beatdown.metagame-clock): eminence discounts every other Dragon spell from the command zone, the per-Dragon payoffs scale with a board nobody else is building, and four-player games trend long enough for that to compound. So the early turns develop and deflect rather than race — which is also what the mana forces, since mean available mana is 4.937 at turn six against 28 of 66 nonland entries costing five or more.
role_assignment.pivot_trigger: The window (strategy:multiplayer.pivot-window) opens on the first turn Aggravated Assault can be activated with a connecting Old Gnawbone or Savage Ventmaw — the two loops the checker has certified (stacks 006 and 003) — or on a Sneak Attack turn with Dragon Tempest, Terror of the Peaks or Scourge of Valkas already down. The doc's bar is 'protection up, interaction counted and accounted for'; the deck holds protection 66.0% of the time by turn six and 77.1% overall, so the bar is usually meetable when the pieces arrive. Note the loop itself is rare: Assault plus a mana dragon assembles 3.6% by turn six, 6.4% within ten turns, mean turn 5.442. Do not wait for it.

gameplan_by_phase.early_t1_t4: Land every drop and take fixing over utility. The land drop holds at 88.3% on turn three and then falls off a cliff — 60.3% on five, 49.7% on six — so a turn-two rock or Farseek is worth more here than in a deck that could afford to miss. Ramp or fixing is in hand 71.6% of the time by turn six. Posture is deflection (strategy:multiplayer.threat-deflection): a five-colour ramp deck reads as slow, and the doc's warning is that experienced tables hit the quiet ramp player anyway — so keep Aggravated Assault, the deck's loudest tell, in hand until the turn it wins.
gameplan_by_phase.mid_t5_t7: This is where the deck is squeezed and where it has to deploy anyway. Deploy in waves under wrath math (strategy:resource-hedging.wrath-math) and buy resilience rather than restraint: Miirym and Lathliss rebuild in tokens, Teferi's Protection and Heroic Intervention cover a whole board, and with Wrathful Red Dragon on the battlefield an opposing Blasphemous Act becomes 39 damage redirected at one opponent (verified, stack 004). Sneak Attack compresses the clock for {R} a Dragon (verified, stack 005), and Hellkite Courser is the deck's only route from the command zone to the battlefield — stack 005 refutes Sneak Attack reaching it (CR 903.6).
gameplan_by_phase.late_t8_plus: The Ur-Dragon is a capstone, not the spine: mean cast turn 8.967, 0% by turn six, and the goldfish does not model the cost reducers, so read that as a floor rather than a schedule. The closers are the Assault engines — Gnawbone funds unbounded combats at net +2 Treasures a cycle and kills sequentially (verified, stack 006); Ventmaw self-funds at +1 mana a cycle (verified, stack 003) — plus the Dragon Tempest burst, which scales with a board the deck has been building all game (verified, stack 001). Sequence the scariest piece last so the deflection budget lasts to the turn you take (strategy:multiplayer.pivot-window).

engines.engine: Treasure-funded unbounded combat phases: an unblocked 7/7 makes 7 Treasures against a {3}{R}{R} reactivation, net +2 a cycle, killing opponents in sequence
Self-funding extra combats: the attack trigger adds {R}{R}{R}{G}{G}{G} against a {3}{R}{R} reactivation, +1 mana a cycle, and the mana survives the phase change
The density payoff: every entering Dragon deals damage equal to your Dragon count, and Ancient Gold Dragon's d20 Faerie Dragon wave widens the count that scales it
Copy doubling on every nontoken Dragon entering — one scaling permanent that out-values a fair board against three seats, and the widener that feeds Tempest, Scourge of Valkas and Lathliss
Sweeper inversion: three triggers of 13 redirected damage kills ONE opponent at 39 or less life, not the table — its real work is making every opposing wipe a bad trade while your tokens rebuild
Velocity: {R} puts any Dragon from hand onto the battlefield with haste, all entry and attack triggers fire, and the damage stands after the mandatory end-step sacrifice

The only card in the 99 that moves The Ur-Dragon from the command zone to the battlefield — hasted for one attack (eminence draw plus a free permanent), returning to the zone with no cast added to the recast tax
engines.evidence: oracle text (cards.json) plus stack 005, which refutes Sneak Attack doing this job

engines.engine: A discount that never has to be drawn or cast: other Dragon spells cost {1} less from turn one, and the attack trigger draws per attacking Dragon and deploys a free permanent when the body is out

engines.piece: Urza's Incubator + Herald's Horn + Dragonspeaker Shaman
engines.engine: The stacked-discount component the deck's own goldfish declaration names its curve fixer — three cards, 19.9% of openers, measured 42.3% assembled and 33.2% by turn six; the thinnest non-combo component in the declaration
engines.evidence: goldfish_targets.json + goldfish_metrics.json targets[0]; the redundancy arithmetic is strategy:deckbuilding.redundancy-vs-tutors ('5 copies is 31% of openers, 7 is 41%')

engines.engine: Virtual card advantage for two mana: you may cast Dragon spells off the top of the library, compounding with the eminence discount so the top card is both visible and cheaper

The second extra-combat effect in the 99: attacking the player with the most life untaps all attackers and adds a combat phase, at no mana — once each turn and conditional on the life-total read, so it hedges the effect without repeating it
engines.evidence: oracle text (cards.json); an oracle-text scan of all 95 entries for an additional combat phase returns exactly two cards, this and Aggravated Assault

key_tensions: Every infinite routes through one card. bracket_report.json lists three two-card infinites and Aggravated Assault is half of all three, so a single Disenchant takes the whole combo plan. The redundancy is thinner than it looks in two directions: Scourge of the Throne is the only other extra-combat effect in the 99 and it is once a turn and gated on attacking the highest life total, and of the seven tutors only Enlightened Tutor can find an enchantment at all — the other six fetch lands, Forests, Dragon creatures or any creature. The doc's prescription for a linear deck is redundancy that shrugs off three answers or a deflection posture that keeps them unspent (strategy:critical-mass); this list has the second, not the first.

The binding constraint is mana, not power. 34 land copies against the 36-38 the template genre asks for (strategy:deckbuilding.ratios), with 28 of 66 nonland entries at mana value five or more, 16 of 34 lands entering tapped in the raw count, and land drops falling to 60.3% on turn five and 49.7% on turn six. Mean available mana is 4.937 at turn six. The source budget is fine — 46 sources against Burgess's 45 — but it is met by rocks and dorks rather than lands, which is exactly why the count passes while the curve does not (strategy:deckbuilding.mana-base). Only five of those sixteen enter tapped unconditionally; the rest are shocks, battle lands and check lands, so the tapland axis itself is comfortable.

Dragon mana cannot pay the combo. Five sources — Haven of the Spirit Dragon, Klauth Unrivaled Ancient, Maelstrom of the Spirit Dragon, Rivaz of the Claw and Unclaimed Territory — read 'spend this mana only to cast' some class of spell, and an activated ability is not a spell (deck-facts notes). None of them can pay Aggravated Assault's {3}{R}{R}, Lathliss's {1}{R} or Sneak Attack's {R}. Klauth plus Assault is a false line no matter how much mana Klauth makes. Treasures are the legal funding route, which is what stack 006 verifies.

The certified kill is not the median kill. The declared infinite-combat component measures 6.4% assembled and 3.6% by turn six at mean turn 5.442, because Aggravated Assault is a one-of and a named card is 7.1% of an opening seven (strategy:deckbuilding.redundancy-vs-tutors). The Dragon payoff component, by contrast, is seven cards at 73.1% and 62.2% by turn six. Prose and play should treat the loop as the ceiling and Tempest-plus-bodies as the median line (strategy:deckbuilding.threat-density separates exactly these).

Colour sources are short everywhere except green. Karsten's 90% budget wants 36 black and 36 red sources against 16 and 27 held; only green clears (24 against 22). Black is a six-card splash so its -20 is nominal, but red is on 32 cards and 47 pips with a maximum of three in a single cost, and nine short is a real number (strategy:deckbuilding.mana-base.color-sources).

Menace versus deflection. The pilot wants the deck to be powerfully scary and the deflection frame says the tells should land the turn they win, not the turn they impress (strategy:multiplayer.threat-deflection). At a bracket-4 table Aggravated Assault gets answered on sight, and the deck cannot re-buy it.

The deck's own sweepers are not free. It holds three mass-damage effects the sweeper axis counts as one: Crux of Fate (whose non-Dragon mode is asymmetric here), Dragonback Assault (3 damage on entry, which all 22 Dragons survive — the lowest Dragon toughness in the 99 is 4) and Blasphemous Act. Dragonback Assault and Crux's non-Dragon mode both kill your only two non-Dragon creatures, Dragonspeaker Shaman (2/2) and Rivaz of the Claw (a 3/3 Lizard Warlock, not a Dragon) — one of the three cost reducers and one of the six castable-dragon pieces. Korlessa, Scale Singer is the 1/4 and is a Dragon; she survives all three.

candidate_missing_lines.title: Cavern-Hoard Dragon + Aggravated Assault: the third contained infinite
candidate_missing_lines.why_plausible: combo_details via deck-facts lists it as a contained two-card infinite producing 'Infinite combat damage to one opponent' / 'Target opponent loses the game' (popularity 9438), and bracket_report.json counts it toward the floor of 4. But its Treasure output equals the number of artifacts the DEFENDING player controls, so unlike Gnawbone the funding depends on an opponent's board — against an artifact-light seat the loop may not sustain the {3}{R}{R}. That is precisely the conditional stack 006 had to settle for Gnawbone.

candidate_missing_lines.title: Do the three cost reducers all reduce The Ur-Dragon, and do they stack?
candidate_missing_lines.why_plausible: The goldfish declaration names a target 'the turn-5-Ur-Dragon hand' and measures it at 33.9%, but nothing here has verified the arithmetic under that name. Incubator and Horn reduce creature spells of a CHOSEN type and the commander is a Dragon Avatar; Dragonspeaker Shaman reduces 'Dragon spells'; eminence says 'other' and so cannot reduce the commander itself. Whether all three apply and stack to {W}{U}{B}{R}{G} is a rules question with a real planning consequence.

candidate_missing_lines.title: Sneak Attack at instant speed: Wrathful Red Dragon in response to a sweeper
candidate_missing_lines.why_plausible: Sneak Attack's {R} ability carries no timing restriction in its oracle text, and Wrathful Red Dragon needs only to be on the battlefield when the sweeper's damage is dealt. If it works, stack 004's redirect becomes a reactive ambush rather than a board state you have to telegraph. The timing window, the ordering against the sweeper on the stack, and whether the redirect resolves before the end-step sacrifice are all unverified.

candidate_missing_lines.title: Miirym + Sneak Attack: does the token copy survive the end-step sacrifice?
candidate_missing_lines.why_plausible: Sneak Attack's delayed trigger sacrifices the creature it put onto the battlefield; Miirym's trigger creates a separate token copy of the entering nontoken Dragon. If the delayed trigger's scope does not reach the token, {R} buys a permanent Dragon body every turn — a large enough rate change to be worth settling rather than assuming.

matchup_frames.vs_sweeper_control: Deploy in waves and buy resilience rather than restraint (strategy:resource-hedging.wrath-math) — the doc's point that against a control deck holding back IS the loss applies squarely, since their plan is the time you would be buying them. Two things make this matchup better than the card counts suggest: with Wrathful Red Dragon on the battlefield an opposing Blasphemous Act is 39 damage redirected at one opponent (verified, stack 004), and Miirym, Lathliss and Utvara Hellkite rebuild in tokens while Teferi's Protection, Heroic Intervention and Flawless Maneuver cover a whole board at instant speed. Let another player's board be the reason the wipe gets cast, then redeploy worst-first and keep the best Dragon for the second one. Sequencing rule that applies in every matchup: Aggravated Assault is the card the table fears and the card you cannot replace, so it is the last permanent you deploy, not the first (strategy:multiplayer.threat-deflection).
matchup_frames.vs_stax: Role flips to beatdown racing the lock's completion (strategy:threat-assessment.resource-denial). Taxes hit hardest exactly where this deck is thinnest — a mana value 5+ top end 28 entries deep on 4.937 mean mana at turn six — so name the piece that beats YOU (an untap denier, or any tax on Assault's activation) rather than the scariest piece on the table, and hold an answer for it. Two things break the tax math: eminence discounts every Dragon spell from the command zone whether or not the commander is castable, and Treasure bursts from Gnawbone, Goldspan Dragon, Atsushi and Cavern-Hoard Dragon convert a single good combat into a turn's worth of mana. Only 3 of the 11 interactive cards are counterspells and a counter answers a lock piece only on the way in — the rest have to be castable under the tax.
matchup_frames.vs_aggro: You are the control seat (strategy:whos-the-beatdown). Their math is the worst at the table — roughly 120 combined life behind three defences makes incremental combat damage a losing plan (strategy:multiplayer.asymmetry) — and 20 fliers with toughness 4 or better blank a ground board outright. Trade time rather than cards, hold single-target removal until the threat is pointed at you (strategy:threat-assessment.answer-economy), and let the engine's inevitability do the work (strategy:whos-the-beatdown.metagame-clock). Crux of Fate's non-Dragon mode is close to a one-sided wipe against a creature deck; the cost is your own Dragonspeaker Shaman and Rivaz of the Claw.
matchup_frames.vs_combo: Held answers rot, and against combo the last profitable moment is their win attempt (strategy:threat-assessment.answer-economy). The suite is real for the job — Counterspell, Swan Song, Dovin's Veto, Deflecting Swat, Chaos Warp, Teferi's Protection — though price Deflecting Swat and Flawless Maneuver at three mana, since their free clause needs a commander on the battlefield and this one is cast on turn 9 on average. You also race credibly rather than purely reacting: all three of the deck's two-card infinites need no extra mana beyond the pieces (mana_value_needed 0 in bracket_report.json), so the frame is pivot-window timing against another clock (strategy:multiplayer.pivot-window). The one class the deck cannot answer is the graveyard — nothing in the 99 touches an opposing one — so a reanimator or a graveyard-loop opponent has to be beaten on speed or on the stack.

distribution_notes: 95 entries / 100 copies; 34 land copies across 29 entries, 66 nonland. The curve peaks at mana value 3 (17 cards) against the format's modal 2, with a heavy shelf of 23 cards at 5-7 and 5 at 8-9 — roughly three times the ~1.5 cards at 8+ that EDHREC data puts in an average deck (strategy:deckbuilding.curve). That is a two-humped ramp curve, and it is the number the mana base has to answer for: 28 of 66 nonland entries cost five or more while mean available mana is 4.937 at turn six and 6.539 at turn ten. Roles (card_roles.json covers 93.7% of the deck): 24 threat:body and 6 threat:tokens, ramp as 6 rocks + 5 cost-reducers + 4 treasure + 3 dorks + 3 land-ramp, 10 value:etb, 7 tutor:narrow, 6 removal:damage, 5 protection:self, 3 counterspell. Six cards carry no role pattern — Aggravated Assault, Chaos Warp, Dracogenesis, Patriarch's Bidding, Rishkar's Expertise, Sneak Attack — and the first of those is the combo plan, which is why deck-audit reads threat-density at 2 against a floor of 3 and card-advantage at 4 against 10 while the deck plainly does both things. Pips are red-dominant: 47 red pips over 32 cards, maximum 3 in one cost, then green 22/20, white 13/12, blue 11/10, black 8/6. Sources held against Karsten's 90% targets: R 27/36, G 24/22, B 16/36, U 16/22, W 15/22. Opening hands keep 75.1% of first sevens at 0.313 mean mulligans and the turn-three land drop holds 88.3%, so the early game is not the problem — turns five and six are, at 60.3% and 49.7%. synergy_graph.json has 132 edges falling inside this deck, but it is a global top-10 shortlist over every tagged card in the format and cannot say how well a card fits this list (deck-facts notes).
overall_assessment: This is a linear critical-mass deck with a combo exit (strategy:critical-mass): every card feeds the Dragon threshold, and past it the deck stops merely outclassing the table and starts taking unbounded combats. Its game is inevitability-ownership (strategy:whos-the-beatdown.metagame-clock) — eminence discounts from turn one, per-Dragon triggers that scale with a board only this deck is building, and six checker-passed stacks covering the burst, the sweeper inversion, the cheat and both Assault loops. Play it as deflect-then-pivot: ramp quietly, deploy in wrath-aware waves, and take one decisive window (strategy:multiplayer.pivot-window) with protection held, which the goldfish measures at 66.0% by turn six. Two honest structural facts shape everything else. The first is that the certified kill is the ceiling and not the median: Assault plus a mana dragon assembles 3.6% by turn six against the Dragon-payoff component's 62.2%, so the deck wins far more games with Dragon Tempest and a board than with a loop, and the loop is carried by one unreplaceable enchantment that five of the deck's own mana sources are forbidden to activate. The second is that mana, not power, is what binds: 34 lands against 36-38, 28 nonland entries at five or more, and land drops falling through 60.3% and 49.7% exactly on the turns the plan has to start deploying. Bracket 4 is earned by contents — three two-card infinites, all assembling at zero extra mana — rather than by Game Changers, of which the deck runs three. That is a coherent identity: menace delivered through engines the checker has already certified, on a mana base that is the first thing worth improving.
gaps: No section treats extra combats as a school in their own right: when to take combat two versus holding the mana, how to price a conditional extra combat (Scourge of the Throne) as a hedge against losing a repeatable one, and how many extra-combat cards a deck built on them should run. strategy:combat-math and strategy:critical-mass are the nearest hits and neither is on point.

No section on kill-order sequencing in multiplayer — which opponent a sequential kill should take first, and what the surviving seats do about it. Verified stack 006 kills in sequence and the doc has no framework for choosing the order; strategy:multiplayer.politics is adjacent but not on point.

No section on cheat-into-play economics (Sneak Attack, reanimation, Hellkite Courser): the cards-for-mana exchange rate, what a sacrifice or bounce clause costs, and when a temporary body is worth a card.

No section on typal payoff density — how many lords and per-type triggers a tribe needs before the tribe is the plan. strategy:critical-mass covers the concept and strategy:deckbuilding.threat-density the finisher count, but neither gives the construction math for a typal deck's payoff-to-body ratio.

strategy:deckbuilding.mana-base gives land counts and a source budget for a generic deck but no guidance on a five-colour base with a top-heavy curve, where fixing and untapped-ness trade against each other directly. The 16-tapped raw count reads as a failure while only 5 of them are unconditional, and the doc has no vocabulary for that distinction.

Nothing in the doc prices a single point of failure. strategy:critical-mass says a linear deck needs redundancy that shrugs off three answers; it does not say what to do when the effect has no second printing your colours can play, which is the actual situation of an Aggravated Assault deck.
